name: Majapahit
summary: A Hindu-Buddhist maritime empire based in East Java, often seen as a forerunner of modern Indonesia, especially under the minister Gajah Mada.

knownFor.label: Gajah Mada’s Palapa oath
knownFor.note: A vow to unite the archipelago.

location.value: Based in East Java around the capital Trowulan. At its greatest extent its influence covered almost the entire Indonesian archipelago (Nusantara), according to the 1365 poem Nagarakretagama.

terrain.value: The fertile Brantas river valley in East Java, with volcanic soils and access to the Java Sea trade routes. Satellite imagery shows canal networks around the capital.

climate.value: Hot, monsoonal tropical climate (described by the Chinese visitor Ma Huan).

resources.value: Wet-rice agriculture, plus control of the spice and sandalwood trade from the eastern islands.
resources.source: Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c. 1200 (2008)

disasters.value: Volcanic eruptions and earthquakes affect Java, but no specific Majapahit-era disaster is documented in the sources checked.

population.value: No overall population figure exists. The Nagarakretagama lists 98 tributary territories.

urbanisation.value: Trowulan was a large brick-built capital. Recent findings (2011) suggest it was larger than once thought. Ma Huan reported 200–300 foreign families living there.

disease.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: Muslim traders settled on Java’s north coast by the mid-14th century (tombstones at Troloyo dated 1368 and 1376). After the fall, Hindu courtiers fled to Bali.

economicBase.value: Wet-rice agriculture in East Java and control of inter-island maritime trade, probably a royal monopoly. Tribute was collected at Trowulan.

tradeRoutes.value: Spices from Maluku, sandalwood from Timor, and rice from Java, traded with China, India, Champa and Malay ports. Chinese voyages (Zheng He, 1405–1433) called at its ports.

moneyAndTax.value: Chinese copper cash coins (kepeng) were widely used, along with native gold and silver coins.

inequality.value: A hereditary nobility and priestly (Brahmin and Kshatriya) elite above commoners. Ma Huan described upper-class widow burning.

governmentType.value: A mandala state, with a central core and looser tributaries, ruled by a Maharaja and governed through a Mahapatih (prime minister).

keyRulers.value: Raden Wijaya / Kertarajasa (1293–1309, founder). Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi (a female ruler, 1328–1350s). Hayam Wuruk (1350s–1389). The chief minister Gajah Mada (mahapatih 1334/1336–1364). Girindrawardhana (c. 1486–1527, last).

succession.value: Hereditary within the royal family, but contested throughout. The deaths of Hayam Wuruk and Gajah Mada were followed by disputes.

institutions.value: A royal council and the office of mahapatih. Provinces were governed by royal relatives (bhre).

stability.value: Early revolts (Ranggalawe, Sora, Nambi, Kuti 1319). The Regreg civil war (1404/1405–1406). A split between rival courts in 1468.

eliteConflict.value: Royal succession disputes after 1389, and the rising power of Muslim coastal rulers, culminating in conflict with Demak (1478–1527).

armyAndTech.value: Large fleets of jong ships, kris daggers and, by the late 15th century, bronze cetbang cannon.

majorWars.value: Used the 1293 Mongol (Yuan) invasion to seize power, then drove the Yuan out. Conquest of Bali (1342–43). The Battle of Bubat against Sunda (1357). A naval attack on Palembang (1377). Wars with Demak (1478–1527).

territoryChange.value: Expanded under Gajah Mada’s Palapa Oath (1334 or 1336) to unite the archipelago. Whether control of distant islands was real or nominal is debated.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals were Sunda, Srivijaya’s successor states, Malacca (supported by Ming China), and Demak.

inventions.value: Jong ships, bronze cetbang cannon, kris metalwork, and red-brick architecture.

scienceEducation.value: Court literature in Old Javanese on palm-leaf (lontar) manuscripts. Literacy was limited to the court and religious elites.

openness.value: Open to foreign traders, including Muslim merchants and Chinese communities, which in the long run helped Islamic coastal states rise.

religion.value: Hinduism (Shaivism) and Buddhism were official, often blended. Islam spread on the coast and asceticism and animism were also present.

languageWriting.value: Old Javanese, written in Kawi script, plus Sanskrit in inscriptions.

artsArchitecture.value: The Nagarakretagama (1365) and Sutasoma (Mpu Tantular, the source of Indonesia’s motto “Bhinneka Tunggal Ika”). Red-brick temples and gates such as Wringin Lawang.

socialStructure.value: Royal family, nobility, Brahmin and Kshatriya elites, commoners and dependants. Details of slavery are not given in the sources checked.

sharedIdentity.value: Remembered in modern Indonesia as a symbol of national unity: the Palapa Oath and the Sutasoma motto are national symbols.
sharedIdentity.source: Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c. 1200 (2008)

neighbours.value: Sunda, Bali, Sumatran states (Palembang, Jambi), Malacca, Ming China, Champa and Ayutthaya.

ideasReligions.value: Visited by Odoric of Pordenone (c. 1321), Ibn Battuta and Ma Huan. Islam spread through its coastal trading towns.

colonisation.value: As overlord, it collected tribute across the archipelago. It was never colonised; it declined before European arrival.

riseSignals.value: Raden Wijaya used the 1293 Mongol invasion to defeat his rivals, then expelled the Mongols. Strong rice agriculture and control of spice trade routes followed.

peakPeriod.value: The reigns of Tribhuwana and Hayam Wuruk with Gajah Mada as chief minister (c. 1330s–1389).

declineSignals.value: Succession conflicts after 1389, the Regreg civil war, the rise of Malacca and Islamic coastal states, and loss of trade income.

outcome.value: Conquered by the Demak Sultanate around 1527, though some sources date the end to 1478. Courtiers fled to Bali, which kept Hindu-Javanese traditions.

sources.value: Old Javanese texts (the Nagarakretagama and the later Pararaton, which often disagree), inscriptions, archaeology at Trowulan, and Chinese and other foreign accounts. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Ricklefs (2008).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate to low. The founding date (1292 or 1293), the end date (1478 or 1527), Gajah Mada’s dates, and how real its overseas control was are all debated.
